questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Matrix Exponent for a Matrix With Distinct Complex Eigenvalues
questions.problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -5 & -1\end{aligned}].$ 

*Hint: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $\pm 3\text{i}.$*

| ${e}^{At}=\frac{1}{3}\,\,$ |  | $3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$ | $2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$ |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |  |
questions.worked_solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -5 & -1\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 2{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -5{\alpha }_{1}t & -{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues or $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=3\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-3\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(3\text{i}t) & ={e}^{3\text{i}t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}\cdot 3\text{i}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+3{\alpha }_{1}\text{i}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}\,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{1}{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-5{\alpha }_{1}t & =-5\cdot \frac{1}{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\cdot t \\  & =-\frac{5}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ -{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-\frac{1}{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\cdot t+\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}=\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ -5\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ -4 & -2\end{aligned}].$ 

*Hint: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $\pm 4\text{i}.$*

| ${e}^{At}=\frac{1}{4}\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | $5\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$ |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$ | {{field-2}} |  |  |
questions.worked_solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ -4 & -2\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 5{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -4{\alpha }_{1}t & -{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues or $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=4\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-4\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(4\text{i}t) & ={e}^{4\text{i}t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}\cdot 4\text{i}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+4{\alpha }_{1}\text{i}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ 4{\alpha }_{1}t=\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}\,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{1}{4t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =2\cdot \frac{1}{4t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\cdot t+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) \\ -{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-\frac{1}{4t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\cdot t+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t))\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}=\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & 5\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & 4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=[\begin{aligned}6 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}].$ 

*Hint: The only eigenvalue of $A$ is $3,$ and it has multiplicity two.*

| ${e}^{At}={e}^{3t}\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $3t$ | $1-3t$ |  |  |
questions.worked_solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}6 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & -3{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=3t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}r(3t)={e}^{3t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(3t)={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{3t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
3t{e}^{3t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{3t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{3t}(1-3t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =6{e}^{3t}t+{e}^{3t}(1-3t) \\  & ={e}^{3t}(1+3t), \\ -3{\alpha }_{1}t & =-3{e}^{3t}t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}1+3t & -3t \\ 3t & 1-3t\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Derivative of a Matrix Exponential
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}],\,{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-2t} & t{e}^{-2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}]
$$

Given the matrices $A$ and ${e}^{At}$ above, compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{At}).$

| $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{At})=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |  |
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{At})=A\,{e}^{At}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{At}) & =A\,{e}^{At} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{-2t} & t{e}^{-2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{-2t} & (1-2t){e}^{-2t} \\ 0 & -2{e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
